newsitem.title: UK: UK minister threatens action if more post strikes.
newsitem.headline: UK minister threatens action if more post strikes.

text.p: Trade and Industry Minister Ian Lang said on Wednesday he would suspend the Post Office's monopoly on mail deliveries costing under one pound if there were any further strikes by British postal workers.

The result of a ballot issued on Wednesday showed some 61 percent of postal workers from the Communication Workers' union voted in favour of continuing strike action. But both sides said they would be holding further talks to resolve the dispute.
Lang said he welcomed the news of the talks. "I hope these discussions will enable an agreement to be successfully and quickly reached," he said in a statement.

But Lang said the ballot did not give the union a mandate to cause misery for the public in the run-up to Christmas, arguing that less than half of those entitled to vote in the union had in fact backed further strike action.
"I would urge the union to sit down responsibly with the Post Office to resolve the dispute before irreparable damage is done, which further strike action would inevitably cause.

"And I must make it clear again that, if the postal service is disrupted by further strikes, it remains my intention, subject to consultation with the Post Office, to suspend the Post Office monopoly for a period of three months."
A suspension would open the way for competitors to grab a slice of the market, in particular from business clients.

The government suspended the monopoly for a month in August this year after earlier strikes. But private companies have found the short space of time too little to mount a serious challenge and are hoping for a complete suspension.
The opposition Labour party said talks were essential.

"We see this as a last opportunity for both sides to get together to resume negotiations to ensure that a satisfactory solution is found, the Post Office is saved from privatisation and the legitimate concerns of both sides are met," Labour's employment spokesman, Stephen Byers, said in a statement. -- London newsroom +44 171 542 6673
